title: 2 Kings 9:30–37
context: Jehu arrives at Jezreel. Jezebel, having prepared herself, looks out of a window and greets him by calling him Zimri, a reminder of an earlier usurper who killed his master (1 Kings 16:9–18). At Jehu’s command, palace officials throw her down, and she dies. When Jehu later orders her burial because she was a king’s daughter, little of her body remains. Jehu interprets this as the fulfillment of the LORD’s word through Elijah (1 Kings 21:23). The text reports these events plainly; readers in both traditions read them as judgment announced by the prophet, without treating the violence as something to celebrate.

verses.text: When Jehu had come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her eyes, and adorned her head, and looked out at the window.
verses.arminianNotes: Jezebel hears of Jehu’s arrival, paints her eyes, adorns her head, and looks out the window. Arminian readers note that the text does not state her motive; many read her preparation as a queen facing her end with dignity or defiance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise refrain from assigning a motive the text does not give, while noting that she meets Jehu as a queen. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, as the narrator presents it, without speculation.

verses.text: As Jehu entered in at the gate, she said, “Do you come in peace, Zimri, you murderer of your master?”
verses.arminianNotes: Jezebel greets Jehu by asking if he comes in peace, calling him Zimri, murderer of his master. Arminian readers note the reference to Zimri, who killed King Elah and reigned only seven days (1 Kings 16:9–18).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her words as a pointed challenge, implying that Jehu’s reign will be as short as Zimri’s. Both traditions read her question as continuing the chapter’s theme of peace, now thrown back at Jehu by the queen.

verses.text: He lifted up his face to the window, and said, “Who is on my side? Who?” Two or three eunuchs looked out at him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu looks up and asks who is on his side, and two or three eunuchs look out. Arminian readers note that the palace officials must choose sides at this moment, and that they decide to support Jehu.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shift of loyalty within the palace as showing how completely Jezebel’s support has collapsed. Shared ground: the verse is a moment of decision for those near the queen, reported without commentary.

verses.text: He said, “Throw her down!” So they threw her down; and some of her blood was sprinkled on the wall, and on the horses. Then he trampled her under foot.
verses.arminianNotes: At Jehu’s command they throw Jezebel down, and she dies. Arminian readers state the event plainly as the text gives it, noting that it fulfills the prophetic word while the narrator offers no praise for the manner of her death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read her death within the judgment announced by Elijah (1 Kings 21:23). Shared ground: both traditions report this verse soberly and decline to elaborate on its details beyond what the text itself says.

verses.text: When he had come in, he ate and drank. Then he said, “See now to this cursed woman, and bury her; for she is a king’s daughter.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu goes in, eats and drinks, then orders her burial because she is a king’s daughter. Arminian readers note the contrast between Jehu’s meal and the death just described, and his recognition of her royal birth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jehu’s order as a measure of respect for her status as the daughter of a Sidonian king (1 Kings 16:31). Both traditions read the verse as showing that Jehu intended a burial, which the next verse shows could not take place.

verses.text: They went to bury her, but they found no more of her than the skull, the feet, and the palms of her hands.
verses.arminianNotes: When they go to bury her, they find only her skull, feet, and hands. Arminian readers note that the text reports this briefly, showing that the prophetic word has come to pass without dwelling on the scene.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outcome as the precise fulfillment of the word that she would not be buried. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with restraint, as the narrative intends, focusing on its link to the prophecy.

verses.text: Therefore they came back, and told him. He said, “This is the LORD’s word, which he spoke by his servant Elijah the Tishbite, saying, ‘The dogs will eat the flesh of Jezebel on the plot of Jezreel,
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu says this is the LORD’s word spoken through Elijah about Jezreel. Arminian readers note that Jehu interprets events through the prophetic word, recalling 1 Kings 21:23, though his wording differs somewhat from that verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment as confirming that God’s word does not fail. Both traditions read the verse as the narrator’s explicit claim that Jezebel’s end fulfilled what the LORD had spoken through His prophet.

verses.text: and the body of Jezebel will be as dung on the surface of the field on Jezreel’s land, so that they won’t say, “This is Jezebel.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu concludes that no one will be able to say “This is Jezebel.” Arminian readers see the end of her influence and memory as a judgment on one who had promoted Baal worship and violence in Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stressing the completeness of God’s judgment on Jezebel. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing words as the end of the unit, without mockery, marking the fulfillment of prophecy.
